THE OM CONNECTION

Measure A 1934 000-28 Before Calling It Short Scale

The original OM-28 and the updated 000-28 are closely related, which makes 1934 a year to measure carefully. Martin’s museum describes the change from OM naming to the updated 000, followed by the 000’s move from long to short scale during 1934. Use the OM-28 identification guide for an instrument carrying the original OM designation.

Use approximately 25.4 inches as the long-scale reference and 24.9 inches as the short-scale reference. The OM-28 history explains the longer predecessor, and the documented 1934 example below confirms the shorter specification. Measure from the nut’s string-bearing edge to the center of the twelfth fret, then double that distance. The saddle is compensated, so measuring only from nut to saddle introduces an unnecessary variable. Record the result in inches or millimeters rather than relying on the owner’s memory of a published specification.

A documented 1934 000-28, serial 57851, provides a useful transition reference: the factory-record account places it in a short-scale batch with T-frets and steel T-bar reinforcement. That example supports the need to distinguish production groups within the year. It doesn’t establish the construction of every guitar stamped 1934.

Also measure the nut and string spacing. Neck width, scale, fret type and reinforcement are separate observations. A replacement fingerboard or neck can make a familiar measurement misleading, so include the heel, fingerboard extension and surrounding finish in the inspection photographs.

A MODEL LIST FOR THE VINTAGE FAMILY

Identify The Size And The Version Of Style 17

The number before the hyphen identifies size. It is part of the model, so an 0-17 and a 00-17 need separate identification. The Martin size decoder explains the numbering and measurements. Count the zeros carefully when reading a worn stamp; a faint impression can disappear under direct glare.

All-mahogany describes the body’s top, back and sides. It doesn’t mean that the fingerboard, bridge, binding or internal components are mahogany. Examine the soundboard’s grain separately from its color. Stain and an amber finish can make spruce and mahogany appear closer in a phone photograph than they do in person.

00-17 / 00-17H	1930s through 1960 original groups	Grand Concert models; later revivals excluded

This list follows the original model descriptions and price groups in the 2026 annual guide, with early construction context from the illustrated Style 15 and 17 archive. It is a list of versions to distinguish, not a claim that every model ran continuously through every intervening year. Rare examples need their own records.

STYLE 15 AND STYLE 17 DETAILS

Compare The Plain Appointments Carefully
Style 15 Evidence

The familiar vintage 0-15 combines an all-mahogany body with restrained ornament. Inspect the rosette, fingerboard markers, bridge and headstock facing together. The Style 15 archive documents wartime tortoise-pattern Fiberloid headstock facings on some 0-15s. An unfamiliar facing therefore needs a period comparison before it is called a replacement.

Joe’s 1955 example gives a different, later reference. Its full front, headstock and block photographs belong to the same instrument. Use them to compare visible parts, while remembering that the exterior cannot establish the installed neck reinforcement or bridge plate.

Style 17 Evidence

Style 17 appointments changed over time, including finish treatment and fingerboard-marker arrangements. Compare a claimed early-1930s guitar with the appropriate production group rather than using a postwar 00-17 as a universal template. The dated construction photographs show a 1937 0-17 and its rectangular bridge.

For a concrete marker comparison, the house construction guide describes paired dots at the seventh and twelfth frets on early-1930s Style 17 examples. Record the fret positions and pairs, then check whether the board or inlays were replaced. A general description of “dot markers” loses that useful detail.

Finish sheen needs particular care. Wear, polishing and later work can alter the appearance of an originally plain surface. The source groups include different early-1930s finish descriptions; a photograph’s gloss level alone cannot settle a transition date or establish that the finish is original.

1955 MARTIN 0-15: HEADSTOCK FACE.

EARLY MODELS AND UNCOMMON CONFIGURATIONS

Inspect A 0-21 As A Concert-Size Instrument

The 0-21 needs its own size and period identification. Early examples can predate routine model stamps, while later entries include uncommon configurations. The early Martin guide explains the construction and marking evidence needed when a serial alone doesn’t name the model.

Joe’s 1930 example shows a twelve-fret body, slotted headstock and belly bridge. The dated bridge archive places that guitar beside other period designs. Its bridge belongs to that particular example; compare other 0-21s with their own period and repair history.

An early guitar’s bridge and top need an assessment of intended stringing and present condition. Existing steel strings don’t establish that a nineteenth-century or early-twentieth-century instrument was built for that setup. Check construction and repairs before increasing tension.

If a seller describes a rare fourteen-fret 0-21 or another unusual order, request the supporting records and measurements. The price source includes isolated configurations, but a listed variant cannot authenticate an unexamined guitar. The model line, body geometry and production evidence must support the specific claim.

1930 MARTIN 0-21: 12-FRET BODY, SLOTTED HEADSTOCK AND BELLY BRIDGE.

brace-note: For a 1944 instrument, confirm the brace profile before using a non-scalloped row: the factory transition occurred late in that year. Read all four columns before choosing a range. Early gut-string groups, later steel-string instruments and New Yorker models have distinct requirements. A nearby date or similar body size cannot substitute for a matching configuration. If the guitar falls outside a supported row, request an individual appraisal.
